title: KaiSip exam mindset principles
description: The reasoning patterns CISA questions reward, grouped into six families. Shared by the web app and the mobile app. Schema: docs/content/PRINCIPLES_SCHEMA.md. Lint: scripts/lint_principles.py.

families.title: Your role
families.question: Who am I in this question, and who owns the decision?

families.title: How you know
families.question: How do I know it is true?

families.title: When it breaks
families.question: What comes first when something goes wrong?

families.title: Reading the question
families.question: What is the question really asking?

principles.title: Recommend, don't implement
principles.rule: The IS auditor assesses, reports and recommends; management designs, implements and owns the fix.
principles.why: An IS auditor who builds a control will later judge their own work, which is a self-review threat. Management owns the process, the budget and the risk, so a fix it did not choose is less likely to last. Advising on what a control must achieve is fine; designing or running it is not.
triggers: asks the IS auditor to design
configure or set up the control

trap.move: Building or configuring the control yourself so the project is not delayed.
trap.why_wrong: It feels helpful, but it is the wrong role. The IS auditor would later audit their own design, and management never takes ownership of the fix.

example.scenario: An IS auditor finds that a new HR system raises no alert when salaries change outside a payroll run. The HR manager asks the auditor to set up the alert.
example.answer: Report the gap and recommend an alert with a named reviewer. HR and IT build and run it; the IS auditor can say what it must catch and test it later.

check.scenario: During a pre-implementation review, an IS auditor finds that buyers can approve their own purchase orders in the new procurement system. The short-staffed project manager asks the auditor to write the approval rule into the workflow.
check.right: Report the gap and recommend an approval rule that the project team builds and the auditor tests.
check.trap: Write the approval rule together with the project team, then report the gap as closed before go-live.
check.why: Writing the rule would leave the IS auditor auditing their own work later. The auditor can say what the control must do; the project team builds and owns it.

principles.nuance: Advisory work is allowed when its scope is agreed in writing up front, management keeps every decision, and the same IS auditor does not later give assurance on it.

principles.title: Independence at every stage
principles.rule: Guard independence and objectivity before, during and after the engagement; never trade them for speed or goodwill.
principles.why: An opinion is only worth something if readers trust that nothing influenced it. Threats such as self-interest, self-review, familiarity and intimidation (undue pressure) can appear at any point, not only at acceptance. So the IS auditor reassesses whenever circumstances change and removes each threat or reduces it to an acceptable level.
triggers: many years on the same client
run the process until someone is hired

trap.move: Treating independence as a one-time check at engagement acceptance, or merely disclosing a severe threat instead of removing it.
trap.why_wrong: Threats that arise mid-engagement still impair the work, and disclosure alone does not fix a severe threat such as a pending job at the auditee.

example.scenario: Two months into an audit of the payments platform, the IS auditor's spouse is appointed head of payments operations.
example.answer: Disclose the new threat to audit management at once. Audit management should assign another IS auditor, have the work done so far reviewed and document the assessment. Independence is not settled at acceptance.

check.scenario: Midway through an audit of procurement, the lead IS auditor accepts a job offer from the auditee's procurement director, starting after the audit ends.
check.right: Report the offer to audit management now, so another auditor takes over and the earlier work is reviewed.
check.trap: Disclose the offer in the final audit report, so its readers can weigh the audit conclusions for themselves.
check.why: A pending job with the auditee is a severe threat that arose mid-engagement. Disclosure alone does not remove it; the auditor steps off and the work so far is rechecked.

principles.nuance: Organizational independence (the reporting line) and individual objectivity are separate tests; a function can be independent while one of its IS auditors is not.

principles.title: Escalate to whoever owns the decision
principles.rule: When an issue exceeds your authority, escalate it promptly to the person or body that owns the decision.
principles.why: Decisions belong where accountability sits: the audit committee for audit independence and critical findings, the project sponsor or steering committee for project risk beyond tolerance, the named authority for invoking recovery. Settling it lower down, or waiting for the next scheduled meeting, leaves the real owner uninformed while exposure grows.
triggers: no one is authorized to decide

trap.move: Handling it yourself: investigating suspected fraud alone, negotiating with the person applying pressure, or waiting for the scheduled report.
trap.why_wrong: Each feels responsible, but none puts the decision with the body that has the authority, and some alert the people involved.

example.scenario: An IS auditor finds that the CIO has granted a relative's company remote access outside any contract. The CIO asks to discuss it privately before anything is reported.
example.answer: Preserve the evidence and escalate through the chief audit executive to the audit committee, which sits above the CIO. Settling it privately leaves the decision with the person involved.

check.scenario: An IS auditor finds that the CFO approved payments to a supplier the CFO secretly co-owns. The CFO asks the auditor to hold the finding while it is sorted out internally.
check.right: Preserve the evidence and take the matter through the chief audit executive to the audit committee.
check.trap: Preserve the evidence and have the chief audit executive give the CFO a deadline to reverse the payments.
check.why: The person involved cannot own the decision. Suspected fraud by a senior officer goes to the body above them, and a private deadline only warns them.

principles.title: Management owns the risk
principles.rule: Management and risk owners accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid risk; the IS auditor and vendors cannot take on that accountability.
principles.why: Accepting risk is a business decision tied to risk appetite, budget and strategy, so it sits with the accountable owner at the level the risk policy names. An IS auditor who accepts risk takes on a management decision and impairs objectivity. A vendor can do the work, but the organization still answers for the outcome.

trap.move: Letting the IS auditor, an operational manager or the vendor accept the residual risk.
trap.why_wrong: None of them owns the risk at the right level. The IS auditor would be judging their own decision, and a contract moves work, not accountability.

example.scenario: A marketing director wants to keep customer data in an unapproved cloud tool for six months and asks the IS auditor to approve the exception.
example.answer: Report the risk and recommend a formal exception decided by the accountable data owner at the level the policy names, with an expiration date and compensating controls. Approving it would make the IS auditor the risk owner.

check.scenario: A business unit cannot patch a legacy server until next year. Its manager asks the IS auditor to sign the risk acceptance form so the exception can be filed.
check.right: Leave the signature to the risk owner and recommend compensating controls until the patch.
check.trap: Sign the form as the independent reviewer and recommend compensating controls until the patch.
check.why: Accepting risk is management's decision. An IS auditor who signs takes on the risk owner's role and would later judge a decision they made.

principles.title: Business goals and governance before technology
principles.rule: Settle direction, policy, ownership and requirements before choosing or switching on a tool.
principles.why: Tools enforce decisions; they cannot make them. Without approved policy, a business case or data classification, a tool automates guesswork and can breach law or block legitimate work. Governance of enterprise IT (GEIT) means IT serves business objectives under direction approved by the board and senior management.
triggers: policy approved by the CISO alone

trap.move: Picking the technical answer first: buying the platform, enabling enforcement or migrating right away.
trap.why_wrong: It looks decisive, but without direction, owners and requirements the tool may solve the wrong problem or create legal exposure.

example.scenario: A CIO wants to buy an AI coding assistant for every developer next week. No policy says what code or data may be pasted into it.
example.answer: Recommend that management first agree on an acceptable use policy and data limits with business and legal stakeholders, then pilot the tool against them. Buying first leaves staff guessing and may leak code or personal data.

check.scenario: A business unit wants to launch a chatbot that answers customer billing questions next month. No one has decided who owns its answers or what customer data it may use.
check.right: Recommend that management name an owner and set data-use limits before the chatbot goes live.
check.trap: Recommend a filter that screens its answers for customer data, plus full logging, before go-live.
check.why: Ownership and data limits decide what the chatbot may do and what the filters must catch. Technical safeguards come after that direction, not instead of it.

principles.nuance: When governance already exists and the gap is purely technical, the technical control can be the right answer.

principles.title: Risk decides where effort goes
principles.rule: Rank by risk, weighing likelihood and impact together, and put effort where combined exposure is highest.
principles.why: Resources are limited, so effort follows risk rather than rotation, preference or the most alarming single factor. Risk combines how likely an event is with how much harm it would cause, after existing controls. A rare event with severe impact can still rank high, but likelihood is weighed, not ignored.

trap.move: Ranking on one dimension, such as the most catastrophic impact or the highest severity score, or covering everything equally.
trap.why_wrong: A single factor misranks exposures, and equal coverage spends scarce effort where risk is low.

example.scenario: An audit manager can cover three of five areas next year. The largest system has strong, recently tested controls; a smaller refunds system has no recent review and rising complaints.
example.answer: Rank the refunds system higher: weak assurance, warning signs and direct financial exposure give it greater combined risk. System size alone does not set priority.

check.scenario: An audit plan can cover one of two areas. Payroll has high impact but strong, recently tested controls. Vendor payments has moderate impact, no recent review and several unexplained duplicate payments.
check.right: Cover vendor payments, where weak assurance and warning signs raise the combined risk.
check.trap: Cover payroll, where a failure would have the greatest impact on staff and the business.
check.why: Risk weighs likelihood with impact. Tested controls lower payroll's likelihood, while duplicates and no recent review raise the exposure in vendor payments.

principles.nuance: A business impact analysis (BIA) deliberately measures impact regardless of likelihood; likelihood is handled in the risk assessment. Neither replaces the other.

principles.title: Understand and scope before you test
principles.rule: Know the business, the population and the risks, then set scope and procedures before testing.
principles.why: Testing answers only the questions planning asked. An incomplete audit universe, an unverified population or an outdated audit program means the work can be flawless yet miss the real risk. When fieldwork reveals something the plan did not cover, the IS auditor updates the plan with audit management's approval rather than ignoring it.
triggers: what should the IS auditor do FIRST

trap.move: Jumping straight into testing, sampling or ranking with whatever list is at hand.
trap.why_wrong: Results drawn from an incomplete or wrong population cannot be projected to the whole, however careful the testing.

example.scenario: Before testing change management, an IS auditor receives a list of production changes from the change tool. Some emergency fixes are known to be applied directly on servers.
example.answer: First build the population from the system side, such as server change logs, and reconcile it to the tool's list. Sampling the tool's list alone would miss the changes most likely to bypass change control.

check.scenario: An IS auditor will test user access reviews for a finance application. IT sends a spreadsheet of user accounts it exported last week.
check.right: Reconcile the spreadsheet to the application's own user table before choosing a sample from it.
check.trap: Test every account on the spreadsheet against its approved request, rather than only a sample.
check.why: Testing, sampled or full, only covers the list it came from. Confirm that the population is complete first, or careful testing can miss the accounts that matter most.

principles.title: Fit the method to the objective
principles.rule: Pick the engagement, test, sampling method or technique that answers what the objective asks, not just a valid one.
principles.why: Each method answers one kind of question. A compliance test (test of controls) shows how often a control fails, a substantive test shows whether amounts or records are misstated, discovery sampling looks for at least one occurrence, and a SOC 1 report covers controls relevant to financial reporting. A well-run procedure aimed at the wrong question cannot support the conclusion.
triggers: which report should the IS auditor obtain
every transaction as it is processed

trap.move: Reaching for a familiar or impressive method: one sample for several objectives, requesting a SOC 2 report for a financial-reporting objective, or periodic extracts when the objective needs real-time detection.
trap.why_wrong: A well-run procedure still fails if it measures the wrong thing. Attribute sampling gives a deviation rate, not a dollar misstatement, and a SOC 2 report is not designed for financial-reporting reliance.

example.scenario: An IS auditor must confirm that no refund over $500 was paid last year without a matching return record. The audit manager suggests a random sample of 40 refunds.
example.answer: The objective is "none", so test the whole population: use generalized audit software (GAS) on a complete extract and match every refund over $500 to a return. A sample can estimate how often refunds lack a match, but cannot show that none did.

check.scenario: An IS auditor must find out whether any vendor in the master file shares a bank account with an employee. Complete vendor and payroll files are available.
check.right: Use data analytics software to match every vendor bank account against every employee account.
check.trap: Select a statistical sample of vendors and check each sampled bank account against payroll records.
check.why: The objective asks whether any match exists. Only testing the whole population can show that none does; a sample can only estimate a rate.

principles.nuance: Cost, tools and staffing decide only among methods that answer the objective. If none is feasible, the IS auditor informs audit management and reports the scope limitation rather than substituting a test that answers a different question.

principles.title: Evidence quality decides
principles.rule: Prefer sufficient, relevant and reliable evidence: from independent sources, obtained directly by the IS auditor and documented.
principles.why: A conclusion is only as strong as the evidence beneath it. Evidence the IS auditor obtains directly, through reperformance, observation or confirmation from independent sources, leaves less room for error or bias than what the auditee says or prepares. More volume does not make up for poor quality.

trap.move: Accepting a written procedure, a management assertion or an auditee-prepared report at face value.
trap.why_wrong: A management assertion needs corroboration, a procedure shows design rather than operation, and a system report needs its completeness and accuracy tested before the IS auditor relies on it.

example.scenario: An IS auditor must confirm that departing employees lose system access within one day. HR says they do, IT offers a ticket summary, and a written offboarding procedure exists.
example.answer: Obtain the termination list directly from HR's system and compare it with the directory's account-disable timestamps. Independent, system-sourced evidence the IS auditor obtains beats statements, documents and summaries prepared by the auditee.

check.scenario: An IS auditor must confirm that nightly database backups ran throughout the last quarter. The database administrator (DBA) offers to help.
check.right: Extract the quarter's job history directly from the backup tool and check each night's run.
check.trap: Obtain a signed confirmation from the DBA, supported by the team's monthly backup reports.
check.why: Evidence the IS auditor obtains directly from the system beats statements and reports the auditee prepares, which need corroboration before the auditor relies on them.

principles.nuance: Relevance comes first: for a specific past event, a contemporaneous system log beats the IS auditor's later re-creation of the process.

principles.title: Materiality takes judgment, not just arithmetic
principles.rule: Judge significance by its effect on decisions, including qualitative factors and small items added together.
principles.why: A weakness is material when it could change what users of the audit report decide. A small amount can still matter if it touches regulatory reporting, repeats thousands of times or shows that a control others rely on has failed. Pervasiveness matters too: a contained issue may qualify the opinion; a pervasive one can make it adverse.

trap.move: Dismissing an issue because each item is small, or because an overall percentage looks healthy.
trap.why_wrong: Aggregation, context and who relies on the figures can make small items material, and averages hide concentrations.

example.scenario: Clerks can adjust shipping fees by small amounts without approval. Each change is under five dollars, but there are thousands a month, and the fees feed revenue reported to investors.
example.answer: Assess the weakness as potentially material: add the items up and weigh who relies on the figures. Calling it minor because each change is small would understate the risk.

check.scenario: Testing finds that a small fraction of supplier invoices were paid without a purchase order. All of them went to one new supplier owned by a purchasing clerk's relative.
check.right: Report it as significant: the concentration and the related party matter more than the low rate.
check.trap: Report it as minor: the rate is well below the tolerable deviation rate the auditor set for the test.
check.why: Significance depends on context, not only size. Exceptions concentrated on a related party point to possible fraud, which a low overall rate hides.

principles.title: Report, agree, then verify
principles.rule: Report findings factually, record management's response, and verify the agreed actions with evidence.
principles.why: An audit adds value only when risks are understood and addressed. Ratings rest on the IS auditor's evidence, so they change for new facts, not for pressure or seniority. Disagreement is reported beside the finding, and closure depends on proof that the agreed action works, not on a promise.

trap.move: Softening or delaying a finding to keep the peace, or closing it because management says it is done.
trap.why_wrong: Both give senior management and the audit committee a false picture; follow-up exists to verify, not to trust.

example.scenario: Management reports that a finding on quarterly access reviews is fixed and sends the updated procedure.
example.answer: Test that the review now operates, for example by inspecting the latest completed review and the access removals it triggered. A revised document shows intent; only evidence of operation closes the finding.

check.scenario: A draft report rates a finding on shared administrator passwords as high. The CIO asks for a medium rating because a fix is already planned for next quarter.
check.right: Keep the high rating and record the planned fix and its date as management's response.
check.trap: Lower the rating to medium and record the planned fix and its date as management's response.
check.why: The rating reflects the risk as it stands today. A planned fix belongs in management's response, and follow-up later checks that it was done.

principles.nuance: If management chooses to accept the risk instead of fixing it, follow-up confirms the acceptance was made at the right level; if the residual risk looks too high, escalate to senior management or the audit committee.

principles.title: Root cause beats symptom
principles.rule: Prefer the fix that removes why a problem happens over one that only handles its effects.
principles.why: Treating symptoms costs money every time the problem returns and hides the weakness that let it happen. Root cause analysis looks past the obvious trigger, such as human error, to the process, tool or design that allowed it. Fix that, and the repeats stop.
triggers: each closed with a separate fix

trap.move: Adding staff, monitoring, reminders or another point fix.
trap.why_wrong: Each is a real action, but it catches the next failure instead of preventing it.

example.scenario: A nightly interface has failed eleven times in three months. Each time an operator restarts it, and management proposes hiring a second night operator.
example.answer: Recommend that IT open a problem record, analyze the failures together to find the common cause, log a workaround in the meantime and fix the underlying defect. A second operator only restarts the job faster.

check.scenario: The same payroll calculation error reappears after each monthly software release. Each time, a developer corrects the affected records by hand.
check.right: Recommend finding why the error returns with each release and fixing the code and its testing.
check.trap: Recommend a reconciliation after each release so that any bad records are caught before payday.
check.why: A reconciliation catches the error every month but never stops it. The defect, and the testing gap that lets it back in, are the cause to fix.

principles.nuance: During a live outage, restore service first; root cause follows through problem management and is never skipped.

principles.title: Prevent first, and build it in early
principles.rule: Prefer controls that stop the problem, designed in early; keep detective controls as a backstop because prevention can fail.
principles.why: Preventive controls act before harm occurs and cost least when built into requirements and design rather than retrofitted. Automated checks apply to every transaction without relying on attention. No preventive control is perfect, though: collusion, override and new threats mean detective controls still complete the picture.

trap.move: Choosing a later review, report or inspection when a built-in preventive control is available.
trap.why_wrong: Detection finds harm after it happens and depends on someone acting on the alert.

example.scenario: A new online banking feature lets customers add payees. The design team proposes a monthly report of payees added from new devices.
example.answer: Recommend that the design include an extra check, such as confirming each new payee with a second authentication factor before its first payment. Keep the report as a backstop; it finds fraud after money has left.

check.scenario: A new expense app lets employees submit claims online. The design team plans a monthly report of claims that exceeded the policy limits.
check.right: Recommend that the app block or route for approval any claim over the limit as it is entered.
check.trap: Recommend that a finance analyst review the monthly report and recover any amounts over the limit.
check.why: A check at entry stops the overpayment; the report finds it after the money is paid. Keep the report as a backstop, since prevention can fail.

principles.nuance: When collusion or management override can defeat a preventive control, a detective control is the right complement.

principles.title: Compensating controls are a fallback, and must be proven
principles.rule: Use a compensating control only when the primary control is impractical, and verify that it actually operates.
principles.why: A compensating control offsets the risk left by a missing control, such as segregation of duties a small team cannot achieve or a patch that cannot yet be applied. It reduces risk only if it is independent, covers the same failure and works in practice. An unverified compensating control is an assumption, not a control.

trap.move: Accepting a compensating control because it is listed on the exception form, or using one when the primary control is practical.
trap.why_wrong: Residual risk may be far higher than management believes, and convenience is not a reason to skip the primary control.

example.scenario: A clinic's only IT administrator manages user accounts and also reviews the access logs. The clinic cannot fund a second IT position.
example.answer: Recommend that a manager outside IT review a monthly report of account changes against approved requests, and test that the review happens and catches exceptions. The administrator should not review their own activity.

check.scenario: An application team asks to skip multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a new admin console and review its login logs monthly instead. The console supports MFA at no extra cost.
check.right: Recommend enabling MFA on the admin console, with a short rollout plan for its users.
check.trap: Recommend the monthly login review as a compensating control, with a named reviewer.
check.why: A compensating control is a fallback for when the primary control is impractical. Here MFA is available and practical, so a later log review is a weaker substitute.

principles.title: Least privilege and segregation of duties by design
principles.rule: Grant only the access a role needs, for as long as it is needed, and separate incompatible duties.
principles.why: Each extra right widens what one mistake, insider or stolen account can do. Segregation of duties (SoD) stops one person from completing a sensitive process alone. Designing both into roles from the start is cheaper and stronger than cleaning up later, with any exception approved, time-limited and covered by compensating controls.

trap.move: Relying on training, trust or an after-the-fact review when one person can still complete the whole process.
trap.why_wrong: Detection and goodwill do not stop a deceived or dishonest person acting alone; segregation of duties does, unless people collude.

example.scenario: Help desk agents can reset any user's password and can also add users to the group that approves payments.
example.answer: Recommend removing group changes from the help desk role and routing them through requests approved by the process owner. Resets are needed for the job; the combination lets one agent take over or create a payment approver.

check.scenario: A warehouse supervisor can record stock counts in the inventory system and also approve write-offs for missing stock. The warehouse has several supervisors.
check.right: Recommend that a different supervisor approve each write-off, with the system blocking self-approval.
check.trap: Recommend a monthly review by the operations manager of all write-offs and the counts behind them.
check.why: One person who can count stock and write it off can hide a theft alone. Splitting the duties stops that; a monthly review finds it after the stock is gone.

principles.nuance: Least privilege is a strong default, not an absolute: emergency access and very small teams are handled through approved, time-limited and monitored exceptions.

principles.title: Operating, not just configured
principles.rule: A control counts when evidence shows it worked over the period, not when it is documented, installed or configured.
principles.why: Policies, settings and tools show design. Assurance needs proof of operation: samples across the period, reperformance, simulated attacks or test restores. Continuous monitoring is management's control and continuous auditing is the IS auditor's; the IS auditor may rely on management's monitoring only after testing it.

trap.move: Concluding from a configuration screen, a design-only report or a tool's dashboard.
trap.why_wrong: These show the control could work at one moment; drift, coverage gaps and unreviewed alerts appear only when operation is tested.

example.scenario: Management says its web application firewall protects the online store and offers the configuration screen as evidence.
example.answer: Ask for proof of operation: confirm it runs in blocking mode, review its block logs over recent months and, with management's approval, run safe test attacks. A configuration screen shows what was set, not that it works.

check.scenario: Management states that every company laptop is encrypted and shows the device management policy that enforces encryption.
check.right: Compare the asset inventory with each laptop's reported encryption status and follow up every gap.
check.trap: Review the policy's encryption settings and confirm that it is assigned to every laptop group in use.
check.why: A policy shows what was set, not what happened. Laptops that never checked in or failed to encrypt show up only when operation is compared with the full inventory.

principles.nuance: Continuous auditing can reduce periodic testing, but neither it nor management's monitoring removes the need for independent evidence.

principles.title: People, containment, evidence, then cause
principles.rule: In a live incident, protect people, stop the harm, preserve evidence, then investigate and recover.
principles.why: Safety comes before systems. While harm is spreading, every minute adds loss, so containment, such as isolating a host or revoking compromised access, comes before analysis. Evidence is preserved as containment happens, because rebooting, wiping or rebuilding destroys what investigators and courts need.

trap.move: While harm is still spreading, investigating, notifying or rebuilding first, or containing in a way that destroys evidence, such as pulling the power.
trap.why_wrong: Investigating while harm spreads adds loss, and destroying volatile evidence can leave nothing usable in court. Contain in a way that preserves evidence.

example.scenario: A sales manager's account is signed in from an unfamiliar country and is downloading the full customer list right now. Legal action is likely.
example.answer: Management should disable the account and end its sessions at once, capturing logs and device evidence under a documented chain of custody. The IS auditor recommends this order rather than acting directly. Interviews, notification and root cause work follow.

check.scenario: An IS auditor reviews the incident plan's first step for ransomware found spreading across file servers. Legal action against the attackers is likely.
check.right: Isolate the infected servers from the network, but keep them running to preserve memory evidence.
check.trap: Power off the infected servers at once, then image their disks as evidence for the legal case.
check.why: Containment comes first, in a way that preserves evidence. Isolation stops the spread; powering off also erases memory that investigators and a court may need.

principles.nuance: Against a stealthy, persistent attacker whose reach is unknown, scope quietly first; visible action too early can push the attacker to hidden footholds.

principles.title: Recover by business priority, and prove it by testing
principles.rule: Let the business impact analysis (BIA) set recovery order and targets, dependencies first, and prove recovery through realistic tests.
principles.why: The business knows how fast harm grows when a process stops, so the BIA sets priorities, recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs); strategy follows. Continuity aims to keep critical services running, even in degraded mode, not only to rebuild afterward. A backup or plan never restored or exercised is a hope, not a capability.

trap.move: Choosing the site or restore order from IT capability, or trusting backup job success messages.
trap.why_wrong: IT-led priorities can recover the wrong things first, and a backup proves itself only when it is restored.

example.scenario: A BIA says online ordering must be back within four hours and payroll within three days. IT's plan restores payroll first because its server is smallest, and no restore has been timed.
example.answer: Recommend reordering recovery to follow the BIA, with online ordering first, then timing a test restore against the four-hour target. Ease of restore does not set priority, and an untimed plan is unproven.

check.scenario: After a site outage, IT plans to restore email first because it is quick, then order processing. The business impact analysis (BIA) ranks order processing as most critical.
check.right: Restore order processing first, with the directory and network services it depends on.
check.trap: Restore email first, so that staff can coordinate the rest of the recovery more quickly.
check.why: The BIA, not speed or convenience, sets recovery order, and shared dependencies come first. The plan's call tree, not email, should coordinate staff.

principles.nuance: Immutable or offline copies matter because attackers target backups, but immutability is one design choice inside a tested recovery capability, not a substitute for it.

principles.title: The priority word decides
principles.rule: Find FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST before reading the options; it decides which true answer wins.
principles.why: Most options in a CISA question are reasonable actions, so the priority word sets the test. FIRST asks for sequence, PRIMARY for core purpose, GREATEST for the worst consequence, MOST LIKELY for probability rather than severity, BEST for the strongest valid choice, and LEAST inverts the test to the weakest option. Answer that test, not the topic.

trap.move: Picking an option that is true and important but answers a different question from the one the priority word asks.
trap.why_wrong: A correct statement still loses if it is not first, not primary or not the greatest.

example.scenario: A question says a business team's SaaS tool may hold customer data and asks what the IS auditor should do FIRST. Options include recommending encryption, notifying the regulator and confirming what data the tool holds.
example.answer: Confirm the facts first: which data, how much and who can reach it. Encryption or notification may follow, but FIRST asks for the step the others depend on.

check.scenario: A question asks for the IS auditor's FIRST step after hearing in an interview that a payroll interface was changed without approval.
check.right: Confirm the change happened by checking the interface's change log and production version.
check.trap: Recommend that the change management policy be updated to cover all interface changes.
check.why: FIRST asks for the step the others depend on. Until the unapproved change is confirmed, any recommendation rests on hearsay.

principles.title: Choosing between the final two
principles.rule: When two survive, prefer the option that comes first, enables the other, fixes the cause and fits your role.
principles.why: Exam writers make the closest wrong choice valid but narrower, later or one step removed. Comparing the final two directly on sequence, dependency, cause and role shows which one the other depends on. Say in one sentence why the best answer beats the closest wrong choice before you commit.
triggers: one option is part of the other
a general rule versus one example

trap.move: Picking the closest wrong choice because it is more specific, more technical or more familiar.
trap.why_wrong: Specific or complete-looking often means later or narrower; the best answer usually comes first or enables the closest wrong choice.

example.scenario: A question about onboarding a new cloud vendor leaves two options: review the vendor's independent assurance report, such as a SOC 2 report, or set the vendor's risk tier from data sensitivity and service criticality.
example.answer: Tiering wins. It comes first and decides how much assurance is needed, including whether the report is enough. The report review is a later, narrower step.

check.scenario: A question asks what the IS auditor should review FIRST when payroll is moving to a cloud provider. Two options survive elimination.
check.right: Review whether the business has defined its security and service requirements for the provider.
check.trap: Review whether the contract includes a right-to-audit clause and breach notification terms.
check.why: Requirements come first and decide what the contract must say. The specific, familiar option is often the later, narrower step.

principles.title: Answer from the question; distrust absolutes
principles.rule: Use only the facts in the question, weigh words like "already" and "small", and distrust "always", "never" and "guarantees".
principles.why: Each fact in the question is there for a reason: phrases such as "already measured", "management has accepted" or "a small team" rule some options out and point to others. Answers built on your own workplace habits, or that promise certainty, ignore that. Correct CISA answers usually depend on risk, so absolute claims are rarely right.

trap.move: Answering what you would do at work, or choosing an option that promises complete or permanent protection.
trap.why_wrong: The question tests the scenario as written, and claims such as one control removing the need for another are almost always false.

example.scenario: A vendor claims its new firewall makes the company's intrusion detection unnecessary. The question asks for the IS auditor's MOST appropriate response.
example.answer: Reject the absolute: one layer cannot remove the need for another, so recommend keeping detection as part of defense in depth. Options that eliminate or remove the need rarely survive.

check.scenario: A question says a company already runs a full weekly backup and asks what would MOST help it meet a four-hour recovery point objective (RPO).
check.right: Add incremental or transaction log backups that run several times a day.
check.trap: Store a copy of the weekly backup offsite at a secure, distant location.
check.why: The stem sets a four-hour RPO, so the gap is how much data could be lost. Offsite storage is good practice but does not shorten the time between backups.
